summary: Specifies the Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold (FROST) signing protocol. A signature can be issued once a threshold number of parties cooperate, spreading trust and adding redundancy for a secret key. It needs only a prime-order group and a hash function, and defines several ciphersuites.

eli5.summary: A vault needing three keys out of five opens only when enough people join. FROST lets a group sign something only when enough members agree.

questions: can schnorr signatures be split among participants
subtitle: A cryptographic protocol for distributed digital signatures.

tldr.problem: Single signing keys create single points of failure. Organizations need to distribute signing authority among multiple parties so that no single compromised key can forge signatures.
tldr.mechanism: FROST is a two-round protocol where participants each hold a key share derived from a shared secret. In the first round, participants generate random commitments. In the second round, given a threshold number of signature shares from different participants, any party can aggregate them into a valid Schnorr signature without knowing the shared secret.
tldr.outcome: Threshold signatures reduce key compromise risk and add redundancy. FROST specifically optimizes for two rounds of communication and works with any prime-order cryptographic group, offering multiple ciphersuites including EdDSA compatibility.

today: RFC 9591 is an Informational RFC from the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG). It represents consensus on threshold signature techniques but is not a standards-track specification. FROST implementations exist in production cryptocurrency systems and research projects; the protocol offers a mature alternative to earlier threshold signature designs.

sections.title: Threshold Signatures and FROST
sections.content:
Unlike single-signer cryptography where one secret key produces signatures, threshold signatures distribute signing authority among multiple parties. FROST (Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold) is a protocol where MIN_PARTICIPANTS out of MAX_PARTICIPANTS must cooperate to create a valid signature on a shared public key.

The protocol depends only on a prime-order group (such as elliptic curves) and a cryptographic hash function. This generality makes FROST compatible with many cryptographic systems. A threshold signature becomes valid only when enough key holders contribute their signature share, making it resistant to key compromise: an attacker would need to corrupt at least the threshold number of participants simultaneously.
sections.eli5: Instead of one person controlling a signing key, a group controls it together. You need enough people to agree (like three out of five) to make a signature work. This way, if one person's key gets stolen, the attacker still can't forge a signature without the others.

sections.title: The Two-Round Protocol
sections.content:
FROST requires two rounds of communication between participants, coordinated by a Coordinator. The Coordinator does not hold any private key material and is untrusted with respect to privacy, but manages the protocol flow.

In Round One (Commitment), each participant generates two random nonces and publishes commitments to those nonces. These commitments are group elements that hide the nonces themselves. In Round Two (Signing), the Coordinator sends the message to be signed along with all participant commitments. Each participant uses their key share, the nonces, and the message to compute a signature share and sends it back. The Coordinator then aggregates all signature shares by summing them, producing a valid Schnorr signature on the group public key.

Nonces are critical: they must never be reused, as nonce reuse in Schnorr signatures allows complete key recovery. FROST protects against this by deriving nonces from both random bytes and the secret key.
sections.eli5: Round one: everyone picks secret random numbers and shares a hidden version. Round two: everyone gets the message, uses their secret piece plus their random numbers to create a signature piece, and sends it back. The coordinator adds up all the pieces to make a real signature.

sections.title: Key Generation and Secret Sharing
sections.content:
FROST itself does not specify key generation, but the RFC provides one method: a trusted dealer using Shamir secret sharing. A dealer generates a random group secret and creates a polynomial f(x) of degree MIN_PARTICIPANTS - 1 where f(0) is the secret. Each of MAX_PARTICIPANTS participants receives the value f(i) for i = 1, 2, ..., MAX_PARTICIPANTS as their key share.

The dealer also performs Verifiable Secret Sharing (VSS) by publishing commitments to each coefficient of the polynomial. This allows participants to verify their key shares are consistent with the public commitments, ensuring they are all points on the same polynomial. Any MIN_PARTICIPANTS shares can reconstruct the secret via polynomial interpolation, but fewer shares learn nothing.

Alternative key generation mechanisms exist outside FROST, such as distributed key generation protocols where no trusted dealer is needed. The key point is that each participant receives a unique identifier (a NonZeroScalar) and a key share, plus the group's public key.
sections.eli5: Someone creates the secret and uses math to split it into pieces (shares) so that any three shares let you recover the secret, but two shares tell you nothing. Everyone gets one piece and a way to check their piece is correct. The public key is shared openly so everyone can verify signatures.

sections.title: Ciphersuites and Compatibility
sections.content:
FROST is instantiated with concrete ciphersuites that specify a prime-order group and a hash function. Five ciphersuites are defined: FROST(Ed25519, SHA-512), FROST(Ed448, SHAKE256), FROST(ristretto255, SHA-512), FROST(P-256, SHA-256), and FROST(secp256k1, SHA-256). The first two are compatible with Edwards-curve signatures (EdDSA), meaning FROST signatures can be verified by software expecting standard Ed25519 or Ed448 signatures.

However, FROST signatures are not deterministic: unlike EdDSA, which derives nonces from the message and secret key, FROST uses fresh randomness in nonces. This is necessary because deterministic nonce derivation in multi-party settings allows complete key recovery attacks. Each ciphersuite also specifies how hash functions with different outputs (like SHAKE256's variable length) are used to map to Scalars in the group.
sections.eli5: FROST works with different types of elliptic curves (like the curves in common cryptocurrencies and secure messaging apps). Each choice of curve and hash function is called a ciphersuite. Some ciphersuites make FROST signatures look like regular EdDSA signatures to the outside world, but they use different random numbers each time to stay secure.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
FROST provides security against Existential Unforgeability under Chosen Message Attacks (EUF-CMA), meaning an attacker who sees signature requests cannot forge a new signature. This assumes the Coordinator and at most (MIN_PARTICIPANTS - 1) participants are corrupted; an attacker controlling the threshold or more participants can trivially forge signatures.

FROST does not provide robustness: a misbehaving participant can cause the signing protocol to fail, resulting in an invalid signature. Identifying misbehaving participants is possible through verification of individual signature shares, but remediation is application-specific. The protocol also does not provide post-quantum security (it relies on the discrete logarithm problem) or downgrade prevention (all participants must agree on the ciphersuite).

Practical considerations include side-channel protections (scalar multiplication must be constant-time), handling of invalid inputs (deserialization functions must reject non-group elements), and nonce security. Participants MUST delete nonces after use and MUST NOT reuse nonces.
sections.eli5: FROST is secure if fewer than enough people collude. If thieves get three shares in a five-out-of-five threshold, they can sign anything. If someone acts dishonestly, the signature might fail, but you can figure out who misbehaved. It does not protect against quantum computers and requires careful implementation to avoid leaking secrets through timing or power usage.

sections.title: Deployment Patterns
sections.content:
FROST can be deployed with or without a dedicated Coordinator. In a single-coordinator model, one entity orchestrates signing ceremonies but does not hold private key material. In peer-to-peer models, each participant communicates with all others, increasing network overhead but removing the coordinator bottleneck.

Applications range from cryptocurrency wallets (where multiple devices or parties sign transactions) to TLS termination (where multiple servers jointly sign transcript hashes) to threshold issuance systems (like certificate authorities split across multiple sites). The flexibility of FROST's design—working with any prime-order group—eases integration into existing cryptographic ecosystems.
sections.eli5: FROST can work with one coordinator managing the signature process, or with each person talking to every other person. You might use it to protect a cryptocurrency wallet with three devices, or to split a company's signing key across different offices so no single office can sign important documents alone.
